Hotels: 44% of chains already automate guest communication

Artificial intelligence is settling into the hotel industry, and it starts with the guest relationship. According to a 2025 global survey of 171 hotel chains included in Statista's Hotels dossier, the most widespread use of AI is automated communication with guests.

Hotels are therefore talking more to their guests thanks to AI. The next question is simple: are they listening better to what those guests say back?

The numbers from the 2025 survey

44% of chains surveyed said they used AI to automate guest communications, making it the most used application. By business area, chatbots and virtual assistants came first at 42%. And among AI solutions, AI assistants were the most widespread, cited by 34% of chains.

These three figures answer different questions in the same survey, which is why they are not identical. But they tell the same story: hotel AI is first used to communicate with guests, before, during and after their stay.

And it is only the beginning. 62% of chains saw AI assistants as the area where innovation would be strongest over the following two years.

Budgets are following

Hoteliers are not just watching. According to a global study conducted in the third quarter of 2024, more than a third of them allocated between 10 and 25% of their IT budget to artificial intelligence. Only a small minority allocated more than half.

These amounts show that AI is no longer a marginal experiment in hospitality. It is becoming an investment line in its own right, and guest relations are its first beneficiary.

In a sector where, according to the same dossier, online channels accounted for 77% of worldwide revenue in 2024, digital communication with guests has become central.

This shows that AI is now part of how hotels plan their technology spending, not a side project led by a single enthusiastic manager.

Answering faster is not enough

Automating communication has obvious benefits: instant answers to frequent questions, booking confirmations, practical information about the stay, availability day and night. Front desk teams gain time for in-person welcome.

But every automated message invites a reply from the guest. And those replies are valuable: special requests, comments on the room, dissatisfaction expressed during the stay, reviews left after checkout. If nobody analyzes them, the hotel talks a lot but learns nothing.

Worse, poorly tuned automation can annoy guests without anyone noticing, because their irritation gets lost in the volume of messages.

There is also a reputation risk. A guest who receives well-written automated messages but whose actual request is not handled remembers it more negatively than if no message had been sent. The promise of a personal relationship creates an expectation that must then be met.

Listening at the same scale as talking

Automatic language analysis lets hotels process guest messages at the same pace they write to them. It sorts feedback by topic (room, cleanliness, noise, food, welcome), measures tone, and flags situations that call for a quick human response.

For a chain, that means comparing properties and identifying recurring problems. For a hotel manager, it means reacting during the stay rather than after a negative review. Our hospitality and restaurants page describes these uses.

The analysis relies on models such as Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case, and data stays hosted in France, never used to train models.

Weekly summaries by property give managers a short list of what to address first, instead of a pile of unread messages.

Over time, they also show whether the changes made actually improved what guests say.

What hoteliers can do now

Three actions are within reach of any property. Gather scattered guest feedback: messages, online reviews, end-of-stay surveys. Measure each month the topics that generate the most negative comments. Check whether automated conversations create satisfaction or irritation.

AI gives hotels the means to talk to every guest. It can also give them the means to listen to each one. That second half is what brings guests back.

These steps do not require a technical team. Above all, they require treating guest feedback as a source of information in its own right, just like occupancy rate or average daily rate.

What this means for you

Hotels use AI to talk to their guests. custovox.ai uses it to listen to them: your reviews, messages and surveys are analyzed by topic and by property, so you know what to improve and can react before a stay ends badly.
